result.markdown: --- engine: knitr --- # Lists ![](/images/shopping_list.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} __Lists__ are used to store multiple items within a single __variable__. __Lists__ allow duplicate values and once defined are always in the same order (__ordered__). Additional items can be added to the __list__ and by default will appear at the end. Finally, __lists__ are indexed meaning that we can easily retrieve the 1st, 2nd....nth item from the __list__. We define a __list__ like any other __variable__. To add multiple values to the __list__ we enclose them in square braces (`[]`) and include a comma between each value. Create the __list__ in the below code block. It consists of made up fold-change values generated by an RNA-Seq type experiment. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} gene_fold_change = [0.25, -0.42, 0.62, 1.27, -0.5, 0] gene_fold_change ``` ::: To add an additional value to the **end** of the __list__, we can use the `.append()` __method__: __Reminder__: Each unique __method__ can only be used on one type of data. The `.append()` method can only be used with __lists__. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} gene_fold_change.append(0.33) gene_fold_change ``` ::: You can create __lists__ containing strings. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} taxonomy_levels = ["Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species"] taxonomy_levels ``` ::: You can even create __lists__ with multiple data __classes__. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} numerals = ["I", 1, "V", 5, True] numerals ``` ::: ## Subsetting data ![](/images/noun-list-5537185.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} A value from a __list__ can be retrieved by the **position** it occupies in the list. This selection can be carried out using square braces (`[]`). This process of selecting a certain portion of data is known as __subsetting__. One of the most vital aspects to grasp for Python is that data structures start at position __zero__. This can be confusing but is a common feature of many programming languages. ### Single values ![](/images/one_hand.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border:white solid 5px" fig-align="center"} To select the first entry in a __list__ we pass position "0" in the square braces: __Reminder__: Create your own informative __markdown cells__. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Get the first value gene_fold_change[0] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Get the fifth value gene_fold_change[4] ``` ::: We can also use a negative value to count from the other end of the __list__. I.e. to get the last value in the __list__. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Get the last value (without knowing the length of the list) gene_fold_change[-1] ``` ::: ### Multiple values ![](/images/four_hand.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border:white 5px solid" fig-align="center"} The same technique also works to select a range of values from the __list__. The upper and lower positions of the range are selected. These are given in square brackets, separated by a colon (`X:Y`). When using a range in this manner: - The first number (`X:`) is inclusive. - The last number (`:Y`) is exclusive. In other words all the positions except the last one will be selected. Try out the following code blocks to see this in practice. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Create a list containing the numbers 1 to 7 one_to_seven = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] one_to_seven ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Subset the third and fourth values one_to_seven[2:4] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Subset the first to fifth values one_to_seven[0:5] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Subset the first value one_to_seven[0:1] ``` ::: If you find this confusing you are not the only one so please don't feel bad about it. It will take time and effort for most people to get used to this. To subset everything from a certain position onwards, leave the upper value blank. This also works to select everything before a certain position. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Subset the sixth value to the end one_to_seven[5:] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} #Subset everything up to (but excluding) the third value one_to_seven[:2] ``` ::: __Lists__ are incredibly useful but have their limitations so it is good to learn other data structures. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: :::
